title: Pip's Lucky Ribbon Mission
markdown:
The Whispering Woods Annual Talent Show had a way of flattening Pip the bunny’s ears. He was to recite a poem about the dewdrop fairy. The poem itself sat neatly in his head. The stage did not. He pictured the bright lamps, the rows of woodland faces, and his tummy performed a small unhappy dance.

“It is only a poem, Pip,” said Marlo the mole, who was his best friend and therefore allowed to rumble such things. “You have practised until the words know their own way home.”

Pip sat on the burrow floor until his ears nearly touched it. “It is not the poem. It is being looked at. What if I forget? What if my voice goes squeaky? What if I lose Grandmother’s ribbon?” He patted his chest. The ribbon, sunset-coloured and (Grandmother had said) spun from bravery, usually lived there.

Marlo patted his paw. “We shall tie it twice. And if you still wobble, I can dig a tunnel under the boards, though I do not recommend arriving mid-verse.”

Pip managed a smile the size of a seed. That night, after fussing with his costume, he left the ribbon backstage beside the velvet curtains. He remembered as soon as he was in bed, which is a useless time to remember a thing.

Morning brought cheerful music and the smell of acorn fritters. Pip’s stomach twisted for a new reason. The show began in two hours, and the ribbon was still among the curtains.

He hurried to Marlo’s burrow. “The ribbon is backstage. I put it down and walked away from it, like a goose.”

Marlo’s whiskers twitched. “Then we shall pop in before anyone else and fetch it. A small secret mission. My favourite kind.”

Pip’s ears flattened. “It is dark in there. The boards creak. The curtains look like large sleepy ghosts.”

“Nonsense,” Marlo said, though kindly. “Think of it as a rehearsal for bravery, with extra dust. We shall be in and out as quick as a wink. My claws are quiet when they need to be.”

They tiptoed to the festival tent under a soft dawn. Marlo nosed the canvas aside. Sawdust and old popcorn met them like forgotten parties. Pip decided the place was secret and almost wonderful, which helped for six steps.

The hall was dim. Dawn made long shadows that played tricks. The stage waited, dark and unused. Blue velvet hung in heavy folds, still as giant caterpillars.

“We find it and we go,” Pip whispered. “Very quietly.”

Marlo led, nudging a fallen cardboard turnip. The floor answered with a creak that seemed far too proud of itself. Pip jumped.

“A loose board,” Marlo murmured. “Come along, explorers.”

They crept onto the stage. The wood groaned in a polite, ancient way. Pip imagined giants underneath and then told the giants they were only joists. Ropes hung like thick vines. A painted moonlit forest on the backdrop drifted in a draught, and to Pip’s wide eyes it looked briefly like someone see-through and shimmering.

He froze. “A ghost. A stage ghost.”

Marlo peered up, then nudged a rope. The painted wood swayed. “Scenery, Pip. Cloth and paint. The breeze is showing off.”

Pip saw that it was true. His heart still drummed. He scanned the dusty boards. The costume basket had been by the left wing, near a stack of crates that did not inspire confidence.

“Over there,” he squeaked, pointing.

They shuffled left. Shadows pulled themselves into worm-shapes. The crates hulked like a creature that had not yet decided to wake. Far off, an owl offered a single hoot that Pip chose to treat as weather.

Marlo sniffed a careful line along the boards and stopped near the edge.

“Aha,” he said, which in mole is a warm sound. He nudged a crumpled sunset of cloth. Pip’s ribbon, a little dusty, entirely itself.

Pip forgot the creaks. He picked the ribbon up. It felt like a familiar hug. He looked at the stage, the curtains, the swaying painted trees. He had walked onto the boards, named the ghost as cloth, and found what he came for.

Marlo’s smile was small and proud. “You did the walking, Pip.”

Pip tied the ribbon at his neck. The knot sat snug. A twitch remained in his nose, but it had changed jobs: it was excitement now. He looked out at the empty seats and imagined the faces that would fill them — neighbours, not judges. The stage was only a stage. He, Pip the bunny, would stand on it and say the poem about the dewdrop fairy, and if his voice squeaked once, the ribbon would still be there.

He took a steady breath. The lamps were not yet lit. He was ready enough.
characters: Pip (a stage-fright bunny), Marlo (a helpful mole)
